title: Rama's name on the stones
hook: a bridge of stones that float because Rama's name is written on them, and the bar that holds a name together
carry: writing god's name is itself a prayer
tomorrow: why is one vowel written before the letter it's sounded after?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: among letters, Krishna is the letter a, and akshara, a letter that's also what doesn't wear away. Today, a look back along the line.

An army stands at the edge of the sea. On the far side is Lanka, and Sita held there. They need a bridge. In a much-loved telling, sung far beyond the old Sanskrit text, the monkeys write one name on every stone, Rama, and the stones float. Valmiki's own Ramayana gives the building to Nala, a monkey engineer; the floating name is the version many grandmothers tell. And yesterday's question has its answer here. The bar across the top of Devanagari holds a word together. Write राम, Rama, and one line holds the whole name.
screen: `A BRIDGE ACROSS THE SEA.` → `RAMA'S NAME ON EVERY STONE.` → `ONE LINE HOLDS THE NAME.`

segments.voice: That bar is the shirorekha, the head line. The letters of one word hang from it together, and where it breaks, a new word starts. Sanskrit often runs words together by sound, so one bar can carry two or three, but a new reader's first move is the same: find the bars. Now the practice the floating stones point to. It's called likhita japa, written repetition. Japa usually means saying a name of God, or a mantra, again and again, often on a string of beads. Likhita japa means writing it. Many Hindu families keep notebooks filled page after page with Shri Ram, or another name of God, a line at a time, and some offer the full notebooks at a temple. The teaching under it is old. Many bhakti teachers say the name of God and God are not two. The name isn't a label; it carries the one it names. That's why, in the story, the stones float, and why a grandmother's notebook is a prayer, not handwriting practice. Now look back along this week, each day on its own bar. Gandhari: where dharma is, there is victory. Mira signing her Lord's name. Bharata carrying sandals home. A hymn that ends on perhaps. Ganesha's pen that wouldn't stop. Krishna in the letter a. Separate words, and one line under all of them: what's sacred, written down and handed on.
screen: `THE SHIROREKHA HOLDS A WORD.` · `LIKHITA JAPA: WRITING THE NAME.` · `THE NAME CARRIES THE ONE IT NAMES.` · `THIS WEEK, WORD BY WORD.` · then, large: `ONE LINE UNDER THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: If you like, take paper, or just a fingertip on your palm. Write a name of God you love, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, or simply Om, once for each slow breath, the way likhita japa is kept, each one on its own line. If you don't pray, write a word that's sacred to you, and let the writing be slow enough to mean it.
Devanagari, still: letters hanging together from one head line, the line that holds a sacred name whole. Year five's word for a while yet.
Hold on to it: writing God's name is itself a prayer. Two days into year five.

howItsDone: Many Hindus keep likhita japa notebooks, writing Shri Ram or another name of God line after line, and people learning Devanagari often start by copying letters under a ruled top line, finding the bar first to see where each word begins and ends.
